description: Vocal and physical choices for Fogg, Passepartout and the ensemble in the play's key moments.
content_html:
The Performer’s Challenge in This Play

No other play on the GCSE set-play list asks more of its performers in terms of physical range. An actor in Around the World in 80 Days may spend one scene as a Reform Club gentleman, the next as an elephant’s front legs, the next as a Yokohama acrobat, and the next as a ship’s captain. Each role requires a distinct physical life — a different physical quality, different proxemics to other performers, a different relationship to the audience. And they must be able to set one down and pick up another in seconds.

This lesson focuses on how to analyse and generate specific performer choices for GCSE exam questions. The key discipline is always the same: translate emotion and character into concrete vocal and physical specifics. Not “Fogg is cold” but “Fogg stands with his weight evenly distributed, spine erect, hands clasped precisely behind his back, gaze level — he does not shift his weight even when Passepartout collides with a customs official.” Not “Passepartout is excitable” but “his centre of gravity is higher than Fogg’s, his movements initiated from the chest rather than the pelvis, his gestures preceding his words by half a beat.”

Key Fact

Fogg’s defining performance quality is stillness: he is the fixed point around which every comic catastrophe revolves. Passepartout’s defining quality is kinetic expressiveness: his body registers everything, instantly. This contrast is not accidental — it is the engine of the play’s comedy.

Playing Fogg: Stillness as Performance

A common student misconception is that Fogg is a comedic character who “acts funny.” The opposite is true. Fogg is the straight man. His comedy emerges from his absolute refusal to react — his deadpan precision is the setup that allows everyone else’s reactions to land. A performer playing Fogg must train themselves to do less: to resist the impulse to react physically, to maintain an even vocal pitch and measured pace even when the scene around them is comic chaos.

In the Reform Club opening, a performer might embody Fogg’s precision by moving only when necessary — each step deliberate, placed as if measured. His gestus (in the Brechtian sense) would be one of meticulous order: he consults his pocket watch not with anxiety but with the calm certainty of a man who believes the universe should conform to his timetable. Vocally, his delivery is measured and even-paced — perhaps a received pronunciation accent delivered at a consistent mid-pitch with minimal variation in volume. He does not rise at the ends of sentences.

As a performer playing Fogg in the moment when he makes the wager with the Reform Club gentlemen, you might choose a slow turn to face the doubters — the full turn taking two counts, unhurried — then a pause of equal length before speaking. Your volume would remain exactly the same as in normal conversation: Fogg does not need to raise his voice to assert dominance. The physical choice of keeping both hands visible and still (not gripping the table, not pointing) communicates total control. Your gaze goes to each face in turn, for precisely the same amount of time, as if ticking off a checklist. This staging choice places Fogg downstage centre in the audience’s field of attention, while the ensemble’s more agitated physical life frames him from all sides, making his stillness more emphatic by contrast.

As a lighting designer for this moment, you might isolate Fogg in a tight spotlight using a profile lantern from directly above while the Reform Club ensemble is lit in a cooler, softer flood. The result is that the audience’s eye is drawn to Fogg’s face and the slight catch of light on his pocket watch — a design choice that underlines his centrality to the story without any camera cut.

Playing Passepartout: Kinetic Engagement

Passepartout is the audience’s emotional proxy — the character who visibly feels everything that Fogg refuses to show. A performer playing Passepartout must master a high-energy physical vocabulary: quick transitions of weight, responsive facial expression, a comedy timing that relies on beat and pause as much as action. His comedy often depends on the delayed reaction: he looks at the audience a half-second after something impossible has happened, sharing his disbelief with them before turning back to Fogg.

Vocally, Passepartout’s French accent is a comic resource (the play is aware of the “excitable Frenchman” cliché and leans into it while giving him genuine warmth). A performer might use a wider pitch range than Fogg — from low conspiratorial mutter to high yelp within a single speech — and a faster default pace that slows only for dramatic effect. In the Hong Kong opium-house sequence, the physical collapse into disorientation requires a performer who can shed their usual body-organisation and move with genuine chaos while remaining technically in control.

Key Fact

Passepartout’s comedy depends on a high centre of gravity, rapid weight transitions and a generous use of audience-facing gesture. He is the play’s emotional thermometer — when the audience sees his face register something, they know how to feel.

Ensemble Work: Trust and Precision

For scenes requiring ensemble lifts and contact work, the company must develop deep physical trust. In the India sequence, when performers form the body of an elephant, any collapse in coordination collapses the fiction. The precision is similar to that required of a circus troupe or a ballet corps — but in this play it must appear effortless, as if the whole company has been doing this for years.

Crowd scenes present a different challenge: blocking a group of eight performers who are each playing multiple roles requires every individual to know exactly where they are at every moment, what their sightline offers the audience, and how their body reads from all angles — particularly important in in-the-round staging. A performer playing a Reform Club gentleman is framing Fogg from one side; as soon as the scene shifts, they must re-enter as a new character from a different part of the stage, taking a new spatial relationship to the action.

Performers in this production must switch vocal quality as rapidly as they switch physical identity. A helpful toolkit: for a British customs official, a clipped, nasal received pronunciation with staccato rhythm; for an Indian elephant-driver (in brief dialogue), a specific tonal warmth and rhythmic pattern distinct from British English; for the Yokohama crowd, fragmented exclamatory sounds rather than fully formed sentences. The key exam principle is that each vocal choice must be specific and must be justified by character context. Vague answers (“I would speak in a foreign accent”) score poorly. Specific answers (“I would deliver the conductor’s three lines in a rapid, high-pitched staccato with a sharp consonant attack, suggesting official authority and impatience”) score well.
exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark performer question, the most common error is to describe the character’s emotional state (“Fogg would feel calm”) without translating it into specific vocal and physical choices for a named moment. You must identify the moment by name, then give at least one vocal choice (pitch, pace, volume, accent, pause) and at least one physical choice (posture, gesture, weight, centre of gravity, proxemics) with a justification for how each choice communicates meaning to the audience. For the 12-mark question on intentions, remember to explain why Eason constructed the Fogg/Passepartout contrast — what is the audience intended to feel, and what does the contrast reveal about the play’s themes?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fogg’s stillness is not a lack of performance — it is a precisely executed choice; his refusal to react is the engine of the play’s comedy and must be described in specific physical terms (spine, weight, pace, pitch) in exam answers.
  • Passepartout’s kinetic expressiveness serves as the audience’s emotional proxy; his physical vocabulary (high centre of gravity, responsive facial expression, beat and pause comedy timing) must be as precisely described as Fogg’s restraint.
  • Ensemble work in this play demands physical trust and precision equivalent to a circus or dance company; blocking, sightlines and spatial awareness are all essential performer skills for a production staged in the round.

practice_questions.text: In Around the World in 80 Days, what is the term for the physical distance between performers on stage, used to signal relationship and status?
Define the term 'gestus' as used in performance analysis.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that gestus refers to the social meaning embedded in a performer's movement or posture; 1 mark for explaining that it communicates character, status or a social/political position through a specific physical attitude.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect on the audience of Fogg's stillness in contrast to Passepartout's kinetic energy. How does this physical contrast generate comedy?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying the contrast between Fogg's stillness and Passepartout's expressiveness (1); explaining that Fogg functions as the straight man (1); explaining how the stillness sets up the comic reaction (Passepartout's energy lands against Fogg's lack of response) (1); explaining the audience effect (delight, surprise, a sense of the world's absurdity bouncing off Fogg's certainty) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Fogg at the moment he is reunited with the Reform Club gentlemen at the London ending, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make to show his unchanged character despite the world-altering journey. Refer to specific performer skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both vocal AND physical choices are specific and named, and both are anchored to the London ending moment. Vocal: measured pace, even pitch, consistent volume (no excitement in the voice — exactly the same as he left); possibly the same rhythm as the opening Reform Club scene to create a structural echo. Physical: the same precise erect posture, the same still hands; possibly the same pocket watch gesture as at the start, creating a circular staging pattern that mirrors the play's circular journey. Every choice is justified with a named effect on the audience (e.g. 'the audience laughs with recognition because his absolute consistency is the joke; the world has changed but Fogg has not').

Secure: At least one clear vocal and one clear physical choice, both anchored to the London ending. Effects are generally accurate. Some use of specific vocabulary.

Developing: Identifies that Fogg is calm and precise but does not translate this into specific vocal or physical choices. Effects implied.

Emerging: Describes Fogg's character ('he is unflappable') without any performer choices or named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in constructing Passepartout as the audience's emotional proxy throughout the play. How does his performance function communicate meaning to the audience?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full analysis of Eason's intentions. Passepartout is designed to feel everything the audience feels: wonder at each location, alarm at each obstacle, warmth towards Aouda, admiration for Fogg. His emotional expressiveness allows the audience to have a relationship with the journey that Fogg's stillness denies. Identifies that his multi-roling also gives him a unique relationship with the audience: he can step in and out of minor roles and return to Passepartout without the audience losing track because his physical signature is unmistakable. Analyses how this dual function (emotional proxy + multi-roling pivot) serves Eason's overall theatrical intention of a co-created journey. Named moments. Named audience effects.

Secure: Identifies Passepartout's emotional proxy function with two or more audience effects. Some named moments. Awareness of multi-roling demands.

Developing: Identifies that Passepartout is 'the funny one' without developing the proxy function or analysing the playwright's intention.

Emerging: Describes Passepartout's character traits without analysing what the playwright intended or what effect this creates.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the Hong Kong opium-house sequence to communicate Passepartout's physical and emotional disorientation. Discuss your performer direction, blocking, lighting and sound choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision. Performer direction: specific physical instruction for Passepartout (how disorientation manifests in the body: loss of controlled centre of gravity, unfocused gaze, slower and less deliberate gesture); the contrast with Fogg's maintained composure when he eventually arrives. Blocking: where Passepartout is placed in the space relative to other performers; how his movement pattern disrupts the usual orderly staging. Lighting: a specific state for the opium house (warm, hazy, possibly a Fresnel with a dimmed, low amber wash; possibly a gobo projecting diffuse shadow patterns to suggest smoke); named effect on the audience. Sound: a soundscape of the opium house (distant voices, a low drone, perhaps non-Western musical fragments); possibly underscore that deliberately disorients through rhythm. Every choice has a named effect on the audience. A directorial statement about what the audience is intended to feel.

Secure: Most disciplines covered, generally concrete choices. At least one named design element and one performer direction. Some audience effects stated.

Developing: Some disciplines covered, choices are partly generic. Effects implied. Limited performer direction specifics.

Emerging: Basic listing with little effect or directorial justification.

knowledge_checks.q: What is Fogg's key performance quality that creates the play's comedy?
options: Exaggerated facial expressions and vocal range
Absolute stillness and refusal to react
Frequent direct address to the audience

knowledge_checks.q: What does 'gestus' mean in performance analysis?
options: A gesture made with both hands simultaneously
The social meaning embedded in a performer's physical attitude
A type of ensemble lift used in physical theatre
A vocal technique involving rising intonation

knowledge_checks.q: Passepartout functions as the audience's emotional _____, visibly registering everything that Fogg refuses to show.
The physical technique in which performers lift or carry each other, requiring precise coordination, is known as ensemble _____ and contact work.
Match each performer skill to its definition.
right: A deliberate pause in speech or movement used to build anticipation or land a comic beat
The organisation of performers in the stage space to communicate status and dramatic focus
The character of a performer's movement: weight, rhythm and relationship to other bodies

flashcard_questions.q: What is Fogg's defining performance quality?
flashcard_questions.a: Stillness — he is the fixed point around which every comic catastrophe revolves.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Passepartout's function in the play's comedy?
flashcard_questions.a: He is the audience's emotional proxy, visibly registering everything Fogg refuses to show.
Social meaning embedded in a performer's movement or posture, communicating character and status.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'physical quality' mean in performance analysis?
flashcard_questions.a: The character of a performer's movement: weight, rhythm, centre of gravity and use of space.

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'beat and pause' in comedy timing?
flashcard_questions.a: A deliberate pause in speech or movement to build anticipation or land a comic beat.
The organisation of performers in the stage space to communicate status and dramatic focus.

flashcard_questions.q: What is ensemble lifts and contact work?
flashcard_questions.a: Physical theatre in which performers lift or carry each other, requiring precise coordination and trust.

flashcard_questions.q: What vocal technique contrasts Fogg and Passepartout most clearly?
flashcard_questions.a: Fogg uses even-paced, mid-pitch, consistent volume; Passepartout uses a wide pitch range and faster default pace.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must performers in this play have especially high sightline awareness?
flashcard_questions.a: The original production was staged in the round, with audience members on all sides.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a spotlight in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: A focused beam of light directed at a single performer or point on stage, isolating them.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Fogg's vocal delivery differ from Passepartout's?
flashcard_questions.a: Fogg's pace is measured and even; Passepartout's is faster, with a wider pitch range.
The physical distance between performers on stage, used to signal relationship and emotion.

glossary_terms.definition: The quality and character of a performer's movement: their weight, rhythm, centre of gravity, use of space and relationship to other bodies.
The physical distance between performers on stage, used to signal relationships, status and emotion.
The social meaning embedded in a performer's physical attitude or gesture, communicating character, status or a social/political position (a term associated with Bertolt Brecht).
A deliberate pause or hesitation in speech or movement used to build anticipation or land a comedic or dramatic beat.
Physical theatre work in which performers lift, carry or support each other, requiring precise coordination and mutual trust.
The organisation of a group of performers on stage into a visual composition that communicates status, energy and dramatic focus.
A specific focused beam of light directed at a single performer or point on stage, isolating them from the surrounding stage.
The area of the stage closest to the audience and in the middle, typically the position of greatest focus and status.
